sources.title: Writing effective tools for agents — with agents
sources.quote: More tools don't always lead to better outcomes. A common error we've observed is tools that merely wrap existing software functionality or API endpoints.

count.note: No number; 'too many tools or overlapping tools can also distract agents'; build a few thoughtful tools targeting high-impact workflows.

grouping.note: Consolidate list_users+list_events+create_event into schedule_event; tools should match how a task is done, not mirror API endpoints.

naming.note: Namespace by service (asana_search, jira_search) and by resource (asana_projects_search); prefix vs suffix namespacing had 'non-trivial effects' on their evals, varies by LLM.

evidence.note: Internal evals (held-out test sets) on Slack and Asana MCP servers: human-written vs Claude-optimized tools, shown in charts only; naming-scheme effect asserted from evals but no numbers published. Not a tool-count sweep.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Says naming/prefix-vs-suffix effects differ by model, so pick by your own evals rather than a universal rule.

sources.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents
sources.quote: One of the most common failure modes we see is bloated tool sets that cover too much functionality or lead to ambiguous decision points about which tool to use.

count.note: Recommends 'a minimal viable set of tools'; no number.

grouping.note: Focus is on non-overlapping tools; 'If a human engineer can't definitively say which tool should be used..., an AI agent can't be expected to do better.'

evidence.note: Field observation, no numbers.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Frames the problem as ambiguity/overlap between tools rather than raw count.

sources.title: Code execution with MCP: building more efficient agents
sources.quote: [paraphrase built from verbatim fragments] Tool definitions overload the context window; presenting MCP servers as code APIs cut usage 'from 150,000 tokens to 2,000 tokens—a time and cost saving of 98.7%.'

count.note: Count becomes irrelevant if tools are exposed as a code API loaded on demand (filesystem of tool modules).

grouping.note: Shifts the question to code-API surface instead of tool list.

evidence.note: Token count of one example workflow (Google Drive -> Salesforce) with direct tool calls vs code execution: 150k -> 2k tokens. Measures tokens, not accuracy vs tool count.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Code-mode approach: cost/context is the main issue, and it is solved by on-demand loading rather than by having fewer tools.

sources.title: Introducing advanced tool use on the Claude Developer Platform
sources.quote: 58 tools consuming approximately 55K tokens before the conversation even starts

count.note: Recommends Tool Search Tool when 10+ tools are available or definitions exceed 10K tokens.

naming.note: Most common failures are wrong tool selection with similar names like notification-send-user vs notification-send-channel.

evidence.note: Anthropic internal MCP evals with large tool libraries: tool search on vs off — Opus 4 49% -> 74%, Opus 4.5 79.5% -> 88.1%. Token count of 5-server setup (~55K for 58 tools). Measures tool search vs all-upfront, not a tool-count curve.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: With deferred loading (tool search) a large library becomes workable; accuracy rises when tools are hidden until searched.

final.recommended_number: use tool search at 10+ tools or >10K tokens of definitions

sources.title: Define tools (Claude API docs: best practices for tool definitions)
sources.quote: Rather than creating a separate tool for every action (create_pr, review_pr, merge_pr), group them into a single tool with an action parameter.

count.note: 'Fewer, more capable tools reduce selection ambiguity.'

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Contrasts with OpenAI Apps SDK (A12) which lists one tool per operation (list/get/create/update/archive).

sources.title: MCP Specification 2025-11-25 — Server: Tools
sources.quote: Tool names SHOULD be between 1 and 128 characters in length (inclusive).

count.note: Spec says nothing about how many tools; tools/list is paginated and list_changed allows dynamic tool sets.

naming.note: 1-128 chars, case-sensitive, A-Z a-z 0-9 _ - . only (no slash), unique within server; examples getUser, DATA_EXPORT_v2, admin.tools.list.

evidence.note: Normative spec.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Spec allows dots and 128 chars, while Claude API regex disallows dots and Vertex AI caps at 64 — portable names should stay [a-z0-9_] and <=64.

sources.title: SEP-986: Specify Format for Tool Names
sources.quote: tool names should be 1–64 characters, case-sensitive, and may include alphanumeric characters, underscores (_), dashes (-), dots (.), and forward slashes (/).

grouping.note: Motivation: 'Allow for hierarchical and namespaced tool names (e.g., using / and .)'.

naming.note: As accepted: 1-64 chars, dots and slashes allowed. Final spec (A8) diverged: 128 chars and no slash.

evidence.note: Standards proposal; status Final.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: The SEP text and the current spec disagree (64 vs 128 chars; slash allowed vs not) — cite the spec, not the SEP.

sources.title: Function calling (OpenAI API guide)

naming.note: Namespaces by domain help when the model must choose between tools for different systems; keep namespace descriptions concise.

evidence.note: Guidance; no numbers published.

sources.title: Block's Playbook for Designing MCP Servers
sources.quote: Combine multiple internal API calls into a single high-level tool.

count.note: No number; Linear MCP went from 30+ endpoint-mirroring tools to grouped get_*_info tools, then to 2 GraphQL tools. Notes 'a trade off between the number of tools and how simple permission management stays'.

grouping.note: Top-down from workflows; upload_file absorbs get_user; Google Calendar list_calendars/list_calendar_events/retrieve_timezone/free_busy -> one query_database (DuckDB SQL); bundle related read-only actions via info_category param, but keep read and write in separate tools (one risk level per tool).

naming.note: Names, descriptions, parameters are prompts - experiment with them; avoid long names (token cost when model must regenerate them).

evidence.note: Experience from 60+ internal servers; before/after case studies with tool-call counts (4-6 calls -> 1) but no accuracy measurement.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Extreme consolidation into generic query tools (SQL, GraphQL execute_readonly_query/execute_mutation_query) is presented as the end state; also warns read+write in one tool breaks per-tool permission approval in Goose/Claude Code/Codex.

sources.title: Comparing Progressive Discovery and Semantic Search for Powering Dynamic MCP
sources.quote: Our benchmarks show that traditional MCP servers with 400 tools consume over 400,000 tokens before the LLM processes a single query.

Success rate only described as 'nearly 100%', not tabulated by count.

sources.quote: the better strategy is to design your toolset around clear use cases and avoid mapping every API endpoint to a separate tool.

sources.title: 4 rules to build an efficient MCP server

sources.title: MCP Tool Naming Conventions for Reliable Agent Tool Selection
sources.quote: MCP tool naming is the interface the planner LLM uses to choose which capability to invoke.

count.note: 'if a server has 80 tools, it is probably two servers'.

grouping.note: Consolidate near-duplicate siblings (read_file, read_file_v2, read_file_safe).

sources.title: How many MCP tools is too many?
sources.quote: Past roughly 40 tools in a single context, even frontier models start picking badly — wrong tool, near-miss tool, or no tool when one would have worked.

count.note: Per agent context, not per server.

grouping.note: Role-scoped agents (split 70-tool monolith into three 15-tool agents), identity-scoped tools, search_tools + run_tool for the long tail.

naming.note: Warns about near-duplicate names (get_user/find_user/lookup_user) across servers.

sources.quote: MCP tools should be basic capabilities – atomic CRUD operations and simple actions. Agents compose these primitives into higher-level workflows.

count.note: 'Every product should be accessible through the MCP server'.

grouping.note: Bad: 'Search for session recordings of an experiment'; instead four tools: list experiments, get experiment, search session recordings, summarize sessions. Workflows go in agent skills.

naming.note: domain-action lowercase kebab-case (feature-flags-list, experiments-create); max 52 chars, CI lint enforces, because of client combined server+tool name limits.

evidence.note: 'agents are better at composing simple tools than navigating complex ones' - no data.

client_limits.as_stated: [paraphrase] Claude Code 64 chars; prefixes tool names with mcp__ + server name
Cursor 60 chars combined server_name + tool_name ; tools exceeding this are silently filtered

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Directly opposite to the 'consolidate into workflow tools' camp: keeps atomic tools and puts workflows in skills/SQL sandbox.

sources.title: Give your agent Neon tools
sources.quote: Progressive discovery (and, on some clients, programmatic tool calling) lets an agent work through a large catalog.

count.note: Large catalog acceptable because hosts now do progressive discovery; clients can narrow via ?category= or readonly.

grouping.note: Hybrid: generated 1:1 Management API tools plus workflow tools (branches.createAndConnect replaces create branch + attach compute + fetch connection string).

naming.note: SDK path mapped to snake_case verb-first names (projects.createAndConnect -> create_and_connect_projects); 'fixed model-facing names and descriptions'.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Reverses its own 2025 position that OpenAPI->MCP is a shaky default: context bloat considered solved by progressive discovery; remaining problem is workflow shape, not count.

sources.title: Building MCP Tools with GraphQL: A Better Way to Connect LLMs to Your API
sources.quote: Each new API endpoint brings in one or two additional tools and the pattern starts to have the LLM act as an API query planner based on these tools.

grouping.note: One GraphQL operation per task-shaped tool; the graph does orchestration instead of the LLM chaining REST tools.

sources.title: Tool Discovery for AI Agents (product page)
sources.quote: If your agent uses fewer than 10 tools, static definitions work fine: context cost is negligible and tool availability is deterministic.

count.note: tool_search + tool_execute replace hundreds of definitions.

evidence.note: Tool RETRIEVAL accuracy, not count vs accuracy: MetaTool nDCG@5 93.8% vs Anthropic Tool Use 91.3% (30-query sample) vs AgentCore 72.8% vs BM25 38.5%; ToolBench Hit@5 74.3% vs 40.0%; ToolRet-full nDCG@10 54.4%; '3.8x cheaper per request' tool search vs all tools loaded over 824 tasks.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Positions tool search as the answer; CTO talk title (WeAreDevelopers 2026) claims tool count, not model quality, is the ceiling (talk itself not fetched).

sources.title: Strata (core concepts)
sources.quote: Too many tools cause LLM choice paralysis

count.note: Treats the 40-50 cap as a coverage gap that progressive discovery removes.

grouping.note: Hierarchy servers -> categories -> actions -> action details, exposed via discover_server_categories_or_actions / get_category_actions / get_action_details / execute_action.

evidence.note: Self-reported: MCPMark pass@1 +15.2% vs official GitHub server, +13.4% vs official Notion server; human eval 83%+ on >2k queries. Compares discovery architecture vs official servers, not tool count.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Argues for exposing hundreds of granular actions behind progressive discovery instead of few high-level tools.

sources.title: The MCP Tool Trap: Why Front-Loading Tools Doesn't Scale
sources.quote: You start feeling the decline in tool calling accuracy surprisingly early, after adding just a handful of tools.

count.note: 'a handful'; front-loading does not scale.

grouping.note: Proposes just-in-time tool retrieval instead.

evidence.note: Cites the 'Less is More' paper on accuracy decline with more tools.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Calls multi-agent splitting a 'mirage'; argues bigger context windows can worsen attention; tool use as a retrieval problem.

sources.title: MCP design is prompt engineering all over again
sources.quote: With MCPs you do the opposite. You compress workflows together because the real optimization target is not architectural purity, but reducing the cognitive and context burden on the model.

count.note: 'you want the smallest possible tool surface area'; went from <10 tools to 5.

grouping.note: get_incident_details + get_server_details + get_alert_rule_details + get_job_details -> get_incident_context; get_available_metrics + get_available_logs -> get_available_sources.

naming.note: Extremely explicit names; namespace tool names because many servers are installed; natural-language time ranges instead of Unix timestamps.

evidence.note: Tested on Gemma 3 4B locally but reports no numbers.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Expects some of these practices to become irrelevant as models change.

sources.title: MCP tool design best practices (SAP Integration Hub)
sources.quote: A high tool count increases the input token volume of tool definitions on every invocation and degrades model accuracy at tool selection.

count.note: 'Prefer fewer, well-scoped tools over a large overlapping catalog.'

grouping.note: Combine back-end steps into one intent-based tool; split catalog across servers by use case/domain; summary vs detail tools for progressive disclosure.

naming.note: Verb-first (get_order_status, find_orders, cancel_order); avoid generic process/handle; natural-language parameter names and enum values (created not CRTD).

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Notes prompt caching lowers cost/latency of tool definitions but does not reduce context size.

sources.title: Stainless MCP (Code Mode) - product page + changelog 'MCP servers now support Code Mode only'
sources.quote: Stainless generates code-mode MCP servers from your OpenAPI spec, letting agents use your SDKs and documentation instead of dozens of endpoint schemas.

count.note: Changelog 2026-01-13: removed all other tool schemes (regular/dynamic).

grouping.note: Code mode: agent writes TypeScript against the SDK in a sandbox; no per-operation tools.

evidence.note: Vendor-claimed evals '94-97% task accuracy, 3x fewer tool calls, 100k+ tokens saved on complex tasks'; methodology, models and baseline not shown on page.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Code mode sidesteps the tool-count question entirely.

sources.title: MCP is Not the Problem, It's your Server: Best Practices for Building MCP Servers
sources.quote: 5–15 tools per server. One server, one job. Delete unused tools. Split by persona. (Admin/user)

count.note: Explicit per-server budget; curate ruthlessly, split by persona.

grouping.note: Replace get_user_by_email + list_orders + get_order_status with one track_latest_order(email); 'Do the orchestration in your code, not in the LLM's context window.'

naming.note: Service-prefixed, action-oriented: {service}_{action}_{resource}, e.g. slack_send_message, linear_list_issues; avoids create_issue collisions between GitHub and Jira.

evidence.note: No experiment; points to Block's MCP playbook and FastMCP material.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Title frames bad servers, not the protocol, as the cause of MCP's problems.

sources.title: Stop Converting Your REST APIs to MCP
sources.quote: every extra endpoint is a tax paid in tokens and latency on every interaction. Second, atomicity is an agent anti-pattern .

count.note: An agent-ready API should be 'ruthlessly curated and minimalist'. Gives no number.

grouping.note: Against 1:1 OpenAPI endpoint->tool conversion. Chaining atomic calls is slow and error-prone, so curate higher-level tools (e.g. a focused find_products(keyword)).

naming.note: Avoid near-duplicate names (agents 'timed out' choosing between create_invoice and generate_invoice). Rename cryptic arguments and hide irrelevant parameters.

evidence.note: Anecdotes from FastMCP GitHub issues; no measurement.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Calls auto-conversion fine for prototyping but not for production agents.

sources.title: too many model context protocol servers and LLM allocations on the dance floor
sources.quote: For the record, Cursor caps the number of MCP tools that can be enabled in Cursor to just 40 tools, and it's for a good reason.

count.note: Criticises VS Code for removing its 128-tool limit: 'Why would you need 128 tools or why would you want more than that?'

grouping.note: The detailed guidance is behind a subscriber paywall.

evidence.note: Practitioner view. The token figures (176K usable, GitHub MCP 93 tools = 55K tokens) are in the paywalled part, as quoted by Simon Willison (C4).

client_limits.as_stated: Cursor caps the number of MCP tools that can be enabled in Cursor to just 40 tools
the removal of the 128 tool limit from Visual Studio Code
client_limits.note: Huntley's claim that VS Code removed its 128 cap is NOT borne out: VS Code docs (updated 2026-10-07) still say 'A chat request can have a maximum of 128 tools enabled at a time.'

sources.title: too many model context protocol servers and LLM allocations on the dance floor (link post)
sources.quote: there is a much more token-efficient way of Interacting with many of these services: existing CLI tools.

count.note: Quotes Huntley: GitHub MCP 'defines 93 additional tools and swallows another 55,000' tokens of ~176K usable.

grouping.note: Suggests small custom CLI tools with --help (including usage examples) instead of many MCP tools.

evidence.note: Cites Huntley's token count (93 tools = 55K tokens). Tokens only, not accuracy.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Says the main cost is context tokens and points to CLI as the alternative.

sources.title: Your MCP Doesn't Need 30 Tools: It Needs Code
sources.quote: an interesting approach is using MCP servers exposing a single tool, that accepts programming code as tool inputs.

count.note: Playwright: 'gets down from ~30 tool definitions to 1'. pexpect has 36 API functions that he would not wrap one-by-one.

grouping.note: Collapse an API surface into one tool that executes code (Python/JS) against a stateful session.

evidence.note: Anecdotal timing only (LLDB debug about 45 s / ~7 tool calls, versus 1 call when re-run from a dumped script). No tool-count accuracy measurement. HN 228 points.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Code mode: a code-executing tool replaces many tools. Follows his earlier 'Tools: Code Is All You Need' (2025-07-03).

sources.title: Model Context Protocol and the "too many tools" problem
sources.quote: Having too many tools exposed in an MCP server can degrade the performances and the output of your LLM!

count.note: Shows one server's tools taking ~22.2% of the context window. No target number.

grouping.note: Build focused MCP servers scoped to user goals or workflows rather than one monolithic server mirroring the API.

evidence.note: Single screenshot of context usage (~22.2%), not a controlled measurement.

client_limits.as_stated: Cursor has an hard limit of 40 MCP tools in total that can be exposed to LLMs ... will only send the first 40 tools
a chat request can have a maximum of 128 tools enabled at a time

sources.title: MCP Server Design: 3 Principles We Learned in Production
sources.author_org: Himamsu Siriseni / Trent AI (dev.to, cross-posted from trent.ai)
sources.quote: Fewer tools, narrower surface. Consolidate around the workflow, not the underlying API. Consistent verbiage everywhere.

count.note: Cut their own server from 17 to 11 tools and saw 'visibly better tool usage'.

grouping.note: The right size for a tool is the workflow the agent performs, not the smallest atomic API operation.

naming.note: 'Same name for the same concept across every input, output, and value on the server.'

evidence.note: Production anecdote (17->11 tools, 'visibly better'). Gives no numbers.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Weak or unknown client models drive the advice ('the model on the other side of the wire is a variable you don't get to pick').

sources.title: Mitigating MCP Tool Limits
sources.author_org: Nate / Apex TI (Substack; promotes their Toolbelt product)
sources.quote: platforms like Cursor impose hard limits on the number of tools available—typically around 40—to manage system resources effectively.

count.note: Example curates 128 raw tools from 7 services down to 24.

grouping.note: Curate tools from several servers into one aggregated server with tailored names and descriptions.

naming.note: Re-name and re-describe curated tools ('tailored names and descriptions').

evidence.note: No measurement. Product pitch.

sources.title: MCP vs CLI: Benchmarking Tools for Coding Agents
sources.quote: The MCP server exposes a single terminalcp tool instead of one per command. This is not just voodoo.

count.note: Recalls old Claude Code docs saying there is a limit to how many tools to expose (he can no longer find the reference).

grouping.note: One multiplexed tool with an action parameter instead of one tool per command.

evidence.note: 120 runs (3 tasks x 4 tools x 10 reps) with Claude Sonnet/Haiku. Compares an MCP server vs a CLI vs tmux vs screen on success, cost, time and tokens (terminalcp MCP/CLI 100%, tmux 90%, screen 67%). Does NOT measure tool count vs accuracy.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: MCP and CLI performed about the same when the tool was well designed. Tool quality mattered more than the protocol.

sources.title: What if you don't need MCP at all?
sources.quote: Playwright MCP has 21 tools using 13.7k tokens (6.8% of Claude's context). Chrome DevTools MCP has 26 tools using 18.0k tokens (9.0%).

count.note: 'That many tools will confuse your agent, especially when combined with other MCP servers'.

grouping.note: Replaces MCP with a few bash scripts plus a README (~225 tokens).

evidence.note: Measured tool-definition token cost of two servers (13.7k/18.0k tokens) against his ~225-token README. Did not measure accuracy versus tool count. HN 237 points.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Argues for CLI or code instead of MCP for coding agents.

sources.title: MCP is dead. Long live the CLI
sources.quote: investing in an MCP server but you don’t have an official CLI, stop and rethink what you’re doing. Ship a good API, then ship a good CLI.

count.note: Argues against MCP in general; gives no tool-count advice.

grouping.note: Notes that MCP forces either dumping large output into context or 'building custom filtering into the MCP server itself'.

evidence.note: No measurement. HN #1, 447 points (posted as 'When does MCP make sense vs CLI?').

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Anti-MCP: CLIs compose (jq/grep), so the context cost lies in the protocol pattern, not only in tool count.

sources.title: Why Your MCP Server Picks the Wrong Tool, and the Five Patterns That Fix It
sources.author_org: AlphaSignal (newsletter) summarising Rodrigues (Celabe) & Vas (U Waterloo), 'MCP Server Architecture Patterns for LLM-Integrated Applications'
sources.quote: Claude Haiku 4.5 picks the right tool 91% of the time when an MCP server shows it 10 tools. Add five more and accuracy falls to 87%.

count.numbers: 10-15 visible tools (Haiku-class); Sonnet 4 >=90% up to 20, below by 30
count.note: 'a single context should stay under roughly 10 to 15 visible tools for a Haiku-class model.'

grouping.note: Five patterns (Resource Gateway, Tool Orchestrator, Stateful Session, Proxy Aggregator, Domain Adapter). Anti-patterns include the 'God Tool' and vague descriptions.

naming.note: Stresses descriptions over names.

evidence.note: Cites the paper's production telemetry from one company (Celabe ANSYR, Q1 2025): ~200 turns per tool-count bucket, tool count vs selection accuracy for Haiku 4.5 and Sonnet 4. Newsletter flags conflict of interest and single-org data.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Warns against over-consolidation too ('God Tool' anti-pattern). Recommends scoped retrieval when aggregating servers.

sources.title: LLM Tools & MCP Are Not REST API: Here's a Better Design
sources.quote: If it's hard for me or the model to pick the right tool because of information overload, the tools become useless.

count.note: Stock-data example merges 8 similar tools into 2. Criticises GitHub MCP's many get_pull_request_* tools.

grouping.note: Merge get_pull_request_comments/_status/_files into a single get_pull_request; combine endpoints that share parameters.

naming.note: Similarly named tools with near-identical arguments confuse models. Differentiate them or merge them.

evidence.note: No measurement.

sources.title: "MCP Sucks" (Until It Doesn't): When Each Wins
sources.quote: The MCP critics correctly identified the problem (bloated, auto-converted MCP servers) but in my opinion they incorrectly blamed the protocol!

count.numbers: GitHub MCP 93 tools ~55K tokens, defaults later cut to 52
count.note: Bloat is a server-design problem. Clients now defer tool schemas.

grouping.note: Avoid auto-converted, endpoint-per-tool servers.

naming.note: Identical tool names across multiple instances (two Slack workspaces) make Claude Code/Cursor route to the wrong instance or suppress one.

evidence.note: Cites a ScaleKit benchmark (75 runs, Claude Sonnet 4: CLI 4-32x fewer tokens, 100% vs 72% success) and Cursor's reported 46.9% token reduction from deferred loading. These are MCP-vs-CLI and token figures, not tool count vs accuracy.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Claude Code and Cursor now 'defer MCP tool schemas by default and load them on demand', which reduces the tool-count cost.

sources.title: MCP is Dead; Long Live MCP!
sources.quote: Don't give your agent complex, useless MCP tools in the first place? CLI and MCP are not mutually exclusive. Be selective in both cases.

count.note: Be selective; gives no number.

evidence.note: No measurement. HN 295 points.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Rebuts Holmes: CLI progressive discovery doesn't save much on complex tasks. Bad tool design hurts both CLI and MCP. Mentions 1M-context windows.

sources.title: A Practical Meta-MCP Architecture for Claude Code: Compressing 60+ Tools into Just Two
sources.quote: the tool definitions alone can consume 36.6k tokens of context. To reduce this overhead, I built a meta MCP server called Code Mode , which exposes only two tools

count.note: search_docs + execute_code replace 63 tools.

grouping.note: Meta-server: a search tool plus a code-execution tool over child servers (code mode).

evidence.note: Measured Claude Code context use of tool definitions: 36.6k tokens (18.3%) before, 4.4k (2.2%) after. Accuracy not measured.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Code mode / search-and-execute replaces exposing many tools.

sources.title: Everything Wrong with MCP
sources.quote: as the servers get bigger (i.e. more tools) and users integrate more of them, an assistants performance will degrade all while increasing the cost of every single request.

count.note: Expects performance to degrade as tool count grows. Notes apps may force users to pick tool subsets.

grouping.note: Says getting query-tool patterns right is hard, and one tool definition does not suit every LLM.

naming.note: Warns about name masquerading/collisions (malicious write_secure_file vs write_file).

evidence.note: Cites Tau-Bench (Sonnet 3.7 16% on airline tasks) for general tool-use reliability. Nothing on tool count. HN 516 points.

sources.title: I Made MCP 94% Cheaper (And It Only Took One Command)
sources.author_org: Kan Yilmaz (personal blog; promotes his CLIHub)
sources.quote: MCP's answer is to dump the entire tool catalog into the conversation as JSON Schema. Every tool, every parameter, every option.

count.note: Cost framing only: ~185 tokens per tool schema.

grouping.note: Proposes lazy loading via CLI --help instead of upfront schemas.

evidence.note: Token arithmetic/estimates for 6 servers x 14 tools: MCP ~15.5K, CLI ~300, Anthropic Tool Search ~500 at session start. Rough estimates, not a controlled run. No accuracy data. HN 324 points ('Making MCP cheaper via CLI').

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Compares with Anthropic Tool Search ('typically drops token usage by 85%'). Treats cost as the problem, not accuracy.

sources.title: Stop Burning Your Context Window — We Built Context Mode
sources.quote: every tool interaction fills the context window from both sides — definitions on the way in, raw output on the way out.

count.note: Cost framing. Focus is on compressing tool output.

evidence.note: Measured output-size reductions (e.g. Playwright snapshot 56 KB -> 299 B, session 315 KB -> 5.4 KB). The 81 tools = 143K figure is stated without method. No accuracy data. HN 570 points.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Tool responses, not just definitions, are a major context cost. Server authors should return compact output.

sources.title: RAG-MCP: Mitigating Prompt Bloat in LLM Tool Selection via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
sources.quote: RAG-MCP significantly cuts prompt tokens (e.g., by over 50%) and more than triples tool selection accuracy

count.numbers: >90% success below ~30 MCP servers; degradation 31-70; near-collapse beyond ~100
count.note: Stress test varies N candidate MCP servers in the prompt (from mcp.so pool of 4,400+); threshold read from a heatmap, not stated in conclusion

grouping.note: Unit is a whole MCP server description, not individual tools

evidence.note: IV1: retrieval vs all-in-prompt ('Blank Conditioning' = all N MCP descriptions at once) vs keyword 'Actual Match'. Qwen-max-0125, 20 web-search tasks, DeepSeek-v3 judge. Accuracy 43.13% (RAG) vs 18.20% (Actual Match) vs 13.62% (Blank); prompt tokens 1,084 vs 2,133.84. IV2: number of MCP servers N in stress test (needle-in-haystack). Small task set (20 queries), single model.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: The 13.62% figure is with ALL servers in prompt at large N on one model (Qwen-max) and 20 queries; often misquoted downstream (e.g., attributed to Anthropic). Units are servers, not tools.

final.recommended_number: >90% below ~30 MCP servers in prompt, collapse beyond ~100 (servers, not tools)

sources.title: How Many Tools Should an LLM Agent See? A Chance-Corrected Answer
sources.author_org: Vyzantinos Repantis, Ameya Gawde, Harshvardhan Singh, Joey Blackwell II
sources.quote: show too many tools and the model struggles to choose.

count.numbers: adaptive avg 2.2 tools beat fixed 5; BFCL: 7 tools ~= 50 tools coverage
count.note: Argues for adaptive per-query shortlist depth chosen by RL, not a fixed cutoff

evidence.note: IV: shortlist depth K shown to the LLM (adaptive BoR vs fixed-K). Benchmarks with 20-3,251 tools (BFCL 370, ToolBench 3,251). BFCL: 90.3% coverage with 7 tools vs 90.8% with 50. Downstream with Claude Sonnet 4.6: gold-tool selection 93.1% at K=2.2 vs 87.1% at fixed K=5; medium-difficulty 76.8% vs 60.9%.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Even going from ~2 to 5 shortlisted tools costs ~6pp choice accuracy on a frontier model - distractor load matters at small K, not just at 100+.

sources.title: Less is More: Optimizing Function Calling for LLM Execution on Edge Devices
sources.author_org: Paramanayakam, Karatzas, Anagnostopoulos, Stamoulis (Southern Illinois Univ., UT Austin); DATE 2025
sources.quote: selectively reducing the number of tools available to LLMs significantly improves their function-calling performance, execution time, and power efficiency on edge devices.

count.numbers: default 46-51 tools per query vs reduced set
count.note: 2024 preprint (DATE 2025) - included as central; small 1.5-8B quantized models only

grouping.note: Uses tool clusters as a search level, not as server design advice

evidence.note: IV: number of tools presented (all 51 on BFCL / 46 on GeoEngine vs dynamically reduced). Models: Hermes2-Pro-8b, Llama3.1-8b, Mistral-8b, Phi3-8b, Qwen2-1.5b/7b (quantized). Reports success-rate gains (e.g. Qwen2-7b ~45%->68% on BFCL per results table, read approximately), execution time -70%, power -40%.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Small local models only; says nothing about frontier models.

sources.title: LongFuncEval: Measuring the effectiveness of long context models for function calling
sources.quote: when the tool catalog is increased to reach a context length of 65,536 and 120,000, the performance deteriorates.

count.note: Degradation 7%-85% as catalog grows; strongest beyond 64K tokens of tools

evidence.note: IV: tool-catalog size (tokens/tool count) and gold-tool position. Models: Mistral-large, ToolACE-8B, BitAgent-8B, Granite-3.1-8B, Llama-3.1-70B, GPT-4o (subset). BFCL-derived simple/live_simple tasks. Mistral-large -94% at 120K; GPT-4o only -12.88%; most -40% to -85%. Also position bias (lost-in-the-middle).

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: GPT-4o was relatively robust - degradation is strongly model-dependent; also measures long tool responses (7-91% drop) and long conversations as separate failure sources.

sources.title: MCP-Zero: Active Tool Discovery for Autonomous LLM Agents
sources.quote: standard schema-injection accuracy on Claude-3.5 plummets from 97.60 to 69.23 (single-turn)

count.numbers: Domain subset vs Full pool (40x more APIs); MCP-tools pool 308 servers / 2,797 tools
count.note: Model requests tools on demand (server then tool, hierarchical)

grouping.note: Hierarchical server->tool routing; relies on server-level descriptions

evidence.note: IV: tool pool size (needle-in-haystack 1 to 2,797 tools) and schema injection vs proactive retrieval. Models: Claude-3.5-Sonnet, GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5-Flash. APIBank: Claude-3.5 97.60% -> 69.23% with full-pool injection; MCP-Zero 95.19%. Tokens ~111 vs 6,308 (60-98% reduction).

sources.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP) Tool Descriptions Are Smelly! Towards Improving AI Agent Efficiency with Augmented MCP Tool Descriptions
sources.author_org: Hasan, Li, Rajbahadur, Adams, Hassan (Queen's University)
sources.quote: Augmented tool descriptions yield a statistically significant increase of 5.85 percentage points in task success rate across domain-model combinations, while causing regressions in 16.67% of cases.

naming.note: Focus is description components (purpose, guidelines, limitations, params, length, examples)

evidence.note: IV: description quality (original vs augmented with six components; component ablations). 856 tools / 103 servers audited: 97.1% have >=1 smell, 56% unclear purpose. Agent runs on MCP-Universe (231 tasks, 202 tools) with GPT-4.1, Qwen3-Coder-480B, GLM-4.5 (+Qwen3-Next-80B): success +5.85pp median, evaluator score +15.12%, steps +67.46%. Dropping Examples did not significantly hurt.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Better descriptions are not free: more steps/tokens and regressions in 1 of 6 cases; examples can be omitted.

sources.title: From Docs to Descriptions: Smell-Aware Evaluation of MCP Server Descriptions
sources.author_org: Peiran Wang, Ying Li, Yuqiang Sun, Chengwei Liu, Yang Liu, Yuan Tian
sources.quote: Across all 10 server groups, the standard-compliant server achieved an average selection probability of 72%, compared to the 20% baseline expected under uniform random selection.

naming.note: Repeated/generic tool names are the most common smell (7,894 cases, ~73% of 10,831 servers) - names must be distinct in a shared agent namespace

evidence.note: IV: description quality of one of 5 functionally equivalent competing servers (10 domains, 1,000 queries, gpt-4o-mini). Compliant server chosen 72% vs 20% chance. Per-dimension gain: Functionality +11.6%, Accuracy +8.8%, Completeness +5.9%, Conciseness +1.5%. Naming prevalence is an audit count, not an accuracy experiment.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Measures competitive selection among equivalent servers (i.e. descriptions as 'SEO' for agents), not task accuracy.

sources.title: Don't Adapt Small Language Models for Tools; Adapt Tool Schemas to the Models (PA-Tool)
sources.author_org: Jonggeun Lee, Woojung Song, Jongwook Han, Haesung Pyun, Yohan Jo (Seoul National University)
sources.quote: Even when appropriate tools are provided in context, models fail to invoke them and instead hallucinate plausible-looking components that are not in the provided schema.

naming.note: Rename tools/params to names the model finds familiar from pretraining (peakedness signal); cuts schema-misalignment errors

evidence.note: IV: tool and parameter NAMES (original vs model-familiar renaming). Models: Qwen2.5-3B/7B, Llama3.1-8B, Llama3.2-3B (+GPT-4.1-mini, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Claude-Sonnet-4.5 comparisons). MetaTool (199 tools) up to +17%, multi-tool +9.6%; RoTBench up to +10.5%; schema-misalignment errors -80%.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: The cleanest controlled evidence that tool NAMES alone move accuracy - mainly for small models.

sources.title: ToolScope: Enhancing LLM Agent Tool Use through Tool Merging and Context-Aware Filtering
sources.author_org: Marianne Menglin Liu, Daniel Garcia, ..., Dan Roth (Oracle / UPenn)
sources.quote: Overlapping tool descriptions, which introduce ambiguity that reduces both retrieval and selection accuracy.

count.numbers: top-k retrieval; BFCL 400, Seal-Tools 4,076, UltraTool 1,885 tools
count.note: Merging redundant tools (-14% BFCL, -25.3% UltraTool) plus retrieval

grouping.note: Automatically merges semantically redundant/overlapping tools into one

evidence.note: IV: tool merging (dedupe) and retrieval vs full toolset. GPT-4o, LLaMA-3.3-70B, Command-R. Correct selection rate +8.8% (BFCL), +34.6% (Seal-Tools), +38.6% (UltraTool); description tokens e.g. BFCL 32,563 -> 469.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Gains bundle merging and retrieval together; overlap, not raw count, is named as the cause.

sources.title: MCP-Universe: Benchmarking Large Language Models with Real-World Model Context Protocol Servers
sources.quote: For all tasks, we connect a total of 7 MCP servers, comprising 94 tools. This configuration introduces additional noise and results in a noticeable decline in performance.

count.note: One ablation adds unrelated servers as noise

evidence.note: Main benchmark (11 servers, 231 tasks; GPT-5 best at 43.72%) does NOT vary tool count. Section 4.5 ablation: IV = extra unrelated servers connected. Claude-4.0-Sonnet Location Navigation 22.22% -> 11.11%; GPT-4.1 Browser Automation 23.08% -> 15.38%; GPT-4.1 Financial Analysis 40.00% -> 35.00%. Small per-domain task counts.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Also finds long context and unfamiliar tools are major failure sources independent of count.

sources.title: MCP-Bench: Benchmarking Tool-Using LLM Agents with Complex Real-World Tasks via MCP Servers
sources.author_org: Accenture Center for Advanced AI, UC Berkeley
sources.quote: MCP-Bench stress-tests retrieval precision by attaching 10 distractor servers to every task, introducing 100+ additional tools per instance.

count.numbers: 28 servers / 250 tools; +10 distractor servers (100+ tools) per task
count.note: Single- vs multi-server tasks compared, but that varies task complexity too

naming.note: Tasks deliberately avoid naming tools (fuzzy instructions)

evidence.note: Not a clean tool-count measurement: distractors are constant across runs; the only comparison is single-server vs multi-server tasks (confounded with task difficulty). Weak models drop (llama-3.1-8b 0.438 -> 0.415; nova-micro 0.520 -> 0.471); gpt-5, o3, qwen3-235b roughly stable.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Frontier models stayed stable with more servers; weaker models degraded.

sources.title: LiveMCPBench: Can Agents Navigate an Ocean of MCP Tools?
sources.author_org: Chinese Academy of Sciences (Mo et al.)
sources.quote: Retrieve errors, on the other hand, largely reflect the limitations of the tool retrieval system, testing its effectiveness in identifying relevant tools based on the server-tool description.

count.note: Uses a retrieval-routing 'MCP Copilot' agent over the whole pool

evidence.note: NOT a tool-count measurement: tool pool fixed, no all-in-context vs retrieval ablation. Measures model task success over 95 tasks: Claude-Sonnet-4 78.95%, Claude-Opus-4 70.53%, most models 30-50%. Retrieval errors the largest failure category (~half).

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Points to retrieval over server/tool descriptions as the bottleneck when tools are many.

sources.title: MCP-Atlas: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Tool-Use Competency with Real MCP Servers
sources.quote: Distractors are typically sampled from the same servers (e.g., google-maps_maps_distance_matrix vs. google-maps_maps_geocode; desktop-commander_get_config vs. desktop-commander_read_file)

count.numbers: 10-25 tools exposed per task, 3-7 needed, 5-10 distractors
count.note: Fixed exposure policy

naming.note: Uses server-prefixed names (server_tool) in its harness, not studied

evidence.note: NOT a tool-count measurement: distractor count not varied. 36 servers, 220 tools, 1,000 tasks. Pass rates: Claude Opus 4.5 62.3%, Gemini 3 Pro 54.1%, GPT-5 44.5%. Tool-usage failures 56.7% of failures; 'no tools called' 36.0% of those.

sources.title: MCPToolBench++: A Large Scale AI Agent Model Context Protocol MCP Tool Use Benchmark
sources.quote: Tool Dispatcher aims to select relevant tools given users' original query, which can help reduce the average number of tools consumed by LLM from Nt(~100) to Nk(~10).

count.note: Design choice, not an ablation

evidence.note: Benchmark of GPT-4o, Qwen2.5-max, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Kimi-K2, Qwen3-coder across 4,000+ marketplace servers; does NOT report accuracy vs tool count - the dispatcher reduction is motivated by context length, not measured.

sources.title: ScaleMCP: Dynamic and Auto-Synchronizing Model Context Protocol Tools for LLM Agents
sources.quote: synthetic queries drive accuracy more than other tool document components

count.note: Agent retrieves tools into memory on demand

naming.note: Tool name gets explicit weight (e.g. 20%) in TDWA embedding, but synthetic example questions matter more than name

evidence.note: IV: retriever type, embedding model, tool-document component weighting (name/description/params/synthetic questions), top-k. 5,000 financial MCP servers, 140k queries, 10 LLMs. Best Recall@10 0.94; tool correctness 23-54%; task completion up to 94.4% (o3 + reranking). No all-tools-in-context baseline.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Measures retrievability of tool docs, not how many tools an LLM can handle.

sources.title: Retrieval Models Aren't Tool-Savvy: Benchmarking Tool Retrieval for Large Language Models (ToolRet)
sources.quote: [paraphrase] All retrievers score under 35% Completeness@10 and under 52% recall@10; ColBERT can underperform plain BM25 on tool retrieval.

count.note: Corpus of 43k tools, 7.6k tasks

evidence.note: IV: retriever model and retrieved vs gold tool set. Downstream: GPT-3.5 on ToolBench-G1 loses 11.40pp pass rate with bge-large-retrieved tools vs annotated tools (50.60 with retrieval). ToolRet-trained retrievers add 10-20% to downstream pass rates.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Retrieval/tool-search is itself a lossy step - shrinking the toolset by retrieval can cost accuracy when the right tool is not retrieved.

sources.title: Tool-to-Agent Retrieval: Bridging Tools and Agents for Scalable LLM Multi-Agent Systems
sources.quote: ensuring that agents and their underlying tools or MCP servers are equally represented without the context dilution that arises from chunking many tools together.

grouping.note: Indexes both individual tools and parent agent/server; coarse server-level descriptions hide tool functionality

evidence.note: Retrieval metrics only (no LLM accuracy). LiveMCPBench (70 servers, 527 tools), 8 embedding models: +19.4% Recall@5, +17.7% nDCG@5 vs prior agent retrievers.

sources.title: Dynamic ReAct: Scalable Tool Selection for Large-Scale MCP Environments
sources.author_org: Nishant Gaurav, Adit Akarsh, Ankit Ranjan, Manoj Bajaj
sources.quote: Our Search and Load architecture with voyage-context-3 embeddings and Sonnet-generated context enrichment provides a production-ready solution that scales.

count.note: Search-and-load meta-tool instead of loading all tools; up to 50% less tool loading

grouping.note: Application-aware hierarchical search tested as one variant

evidence.note: IV: five tool-selection architectures and embedding models. Top-5 retrieval accuracy 40% (text-embedding-3-large) -> 60% (voyage-context-3 + Sonnet 4 enrichment), Top-10 68%. Mostly retrieval metrics; tool count not varied.

sources.title: Hammer: Robust Function-Calling for On-Device Language Models via Function Masking
sources.author_org: Lin et al. (Huawei Noah's Ark / SJTU)
sources.quote: This result confirms the model's overreliance on function and parameter names, highlighting the potential risks this behavior may pose in real-world applications.

count.note: 2024 - included only as naming evidence

naming.note: Models lean on names over descriptions; misleading/unfamiliar names hurt

evidence.note: IV: function/parameter names masked with random strings. xLAM-1B-fc on Seal-Tools drops substantially; Hammer (trained with masking) barely changes. Small models only.

sources.title: Benchmarking Single Agent Performance
sources.quote: Both more context and more tools degrade agent performance

count.note: No number; motivates splitting work across agents (multi-agent) rather than one agent with all domains.

grouping.note: Groups tools by domain only as an experimental unit.

evidence.note: IV: number of domains (each adds instructions + tools) given to one ReAct agent, 1 to 14+ domains. Models: Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o, o1, o3-mini, Llama-3.3-70B. Calendar task: o1 71% -> ~40% at 7 domains, o3-mini 68% -> ~15%, GPT-4o -> 2% at 7 domains, Claude 3.5 Sonnet ~50% -> ~40% at 14. Confounds tool count with added instructions/context.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Degradation strongly model-dependent: Claude 3.5 Sonnet / o1 held up far better than GPT-4o / Llama. Tool count is confounded with instruction length.

sources.title: MCP Server Architecture Patterns for LLM-Integrated Applications
sources.quote: [paraphrase of section VI-C] when a single MCP server exposes more than about 10-15 tools, use the scoped Proxy Aggregator so only relevant subsets appear per context

count.note: Accuracy drops below 90% between 10 and 15 tools (Haiku 4.5) and between 20 and 30 (Sonnet 4).

grouping.note: Five patterns; 'God Tool' anti-pattern: do not hide many actions behind one undifferentiated schema - decompose into distinct named tools; scope subsets per context.

evidence.note: IV: tools visible per context, buckets {1,3,5,10,15,20,30,50}; 200 production turns per bucket from one company's voice-AI platform (ANSYR, Q1 2025); Claude Haiku 4.5 and Sonnet 4; human-confirmed ground truth; Wilson CI +/-4pp. Haiku 91% @10 -> 87% @15. Author works for the platform operator.

sources.contrarian_or_nuance: Warns against over-consolidation (God Tool) as much as against too many tools.

sources.title: How to Fix Your Context (companion to 'How Long Contexts Fail')
sources.quote: selecting the right tools becomes critical when you have more than 30 tools ... Beyond 100 tools, the model was virtually guaranteed to fail.

count.numbers: 30 / 100 (DeepSeek-v3, from RAG-MCP); 19 vs 46 (Llama 3.1 8B, from Less is More)
count.note: 'Tool loadout': pick a few hand-curated tools, or retrieve tools per task (RAG over tool descriptions).
